title: Ames: free choice acts as 'principle which' in pious works, not as 'principle by which'
source_text: XLVI. Ideoque ad quaestionem An homines per liberum arbitrium agant in operibus pietatis, Respondet, si phrasis illa agere per liberum arbitrium, significat liberum arbitrium in istis operibus agere ut principium quod, illam a nobis admitti: si vero significet libertatem naturalem esse principium quo actionis spiritualis, non vero accipere & posse & velle suum a gratia, eam a nobis rejici tanquam Pelagianam. Lib. 4. de Libr. Arbitr. cap. 3. de viribus liberi arbitrii.
pass_a_gloss: XLVI. And therefore to the question Whether men act through free choice in works of piety, He answers, if that phrase to act through free choice, signifies that free choice acts in those works as the principle which, that it is admitted by us: but if it signify that natural freedom is the principle by which of spiritual action, and does not receive both its power and its will from grace, that it is rejected by us as Pelagian. Book 4. on Free Choice chap. 3. on the strength of free choice.
pass_b_english: So when asked whether men act through free choice in works of piety, he answers as follows. If 'acting through free choice' means that free choice acts in those works as the principle that acts (principium quod), we accept it.

If it means that natural freedom is the principle by which (principium quo) a spiritual action is done, and does not receive both its ability and its willing from grace, we reject it as Pelagian. Book 4, on free choice, chapter 3, on the powers of free choice.
